title: Renderer, shader, material, instance
notes: A texture stores sampled data. A material describes how to use that data. A shader is the executable calculation; the renderer coordinates the whole image. title: Where the material enters a rendered image
notes: The pre-assessment asked for the logical order: scene submission, vertex processing, rasterization, pixel or fragment processing, then final pixels. In Unreal, World Position Offset changes vertex positions; a material’s Base Color participates in later surface shading. Ned will explain coverage, depth and interpolation. title: Coordinates tell the shader where to look
notes: If a checker texture becomes stretched on part of a mesh, inspect the UV mapping before blaming texture resolution. UVs are sampling addresses; local and world positions are different coordinate frames. A direction is not a position: translation affects points, not direction vectors. Unreal distinguishes Transform from TransformPosition. Compare vectors in the same space. For this class the texture-flow lesson changes UVs, while World Position Offset changes geometry. Those are different mechanisms even when both suggest moving water.

title: Normals and dot products: predict the signal
notes: A normal describes surface orientation; normalizing is an operation that makes a nonzero vector length one. These are different ideas. For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine of their angle: one for matching directions, zero at a right angle, and minus one for opposite directions. Unreal world Up is positive Z. A sideways-facing normal has zero dot with Up. This same reasoning will drive our light bands and view-angle edges. Normalize both inputs and put them in the same coordinate space. Reversing a cross product reverses its direction, which matters when constructing normals from triangle edges. Do not normalize a zero vector as a direction. Which faces would a positive world-Up mask select?

title: A frame budget is a measured time budget
notes: In the pre-assessment example, the GPU takes 24 milliseconds and the CPU takes nine. Their work can overlap, so do not simply add them as a general frame-time rule. At a 60 FPS target the GPU exceeds the 16.7 millisecond budget. If translucency is measured at eleven milliseconds, investigate that pass and compare a controlled change. A debug color has meaning only within its named visualization mode; red is not a universal measurement of cost. We will do the detailed profiling work in Week 9.

title: Color building blocks
notes: Reference page; no need to teach every row during the lecture. Multiply / Add: Multiplication is component-wise. A scalar scales every component. Multiplying by white preserves RGB; by black removes it. Mix / Lerp: Alpha 0 returns A; 1 returns B. Values outside 0..1 extrapolate. A color Alpha blends channels independently. Clamp / Saturate: Clamping is not normalization or remapping: values outside the range collapse to the endpoints.

title: Masks and repeating values
notes: Reference page; no need to teach every row during the lecture. Step: Result is 0 when x < edge and 1 otherwise. UE Step uses X for the value and Y for the edge; the code arguments put the edge first. Smoothstep: Keep Min < Max. This softens a value transition; it does not blur a texture or guarantee anti-aliasing. Fract / Frac: Result is x − floor(x), also for negative x. Explicit Frac creates derivative discontinuities; texture wrapping usually handles repeating UVs better.

title: Lighting building blocks
notes: Reference page; no need to teach every row during the lecture. Normalize + Dot: Use nonzero vectors in the same space. L points toward the light. Dot of unit vectors ranges from -1 to 1 before clamping. Power + view rim: Normalize N and V first. Higher positive power narrows the rim. This artistic mask alone is not a complete Fresnel reflectance model. UE Fresnel adds its own BaseReflectFractionIn parameter and expects a world-space normal. Floor + bands: x is clamped 0..1 and n is an integer ≥2. The Min keeps x=1 at the final level rather than making an extra band.

title: Motion and shader stages
notes: Reference page; no need to teach every row during the lecture. Sine / Cosine: Code sin/cos use radians. UE Sine/Cosine default Period is 1: an input of 1 completes a cycle. Alternatively divide radians by 2π and keep Period 1. Vertex displacement: The GLSL example assumes a local +Z plane. UE WPO uses world units (normally cm), needs enough vertices, and does not automatically update collision. Vertex displacement also needs matching shading normals. DDX / DDY / Fwidth: These are screen derivatives, not an analytic object-space slope. Use in the pixel stage. Discontinuous control flow or values can make them unreliable.
